articles.title: How Iran's Pegah Ahangarani Turned Her Family Archives Into a Regime-Challenging Oscar Hopeful
articles.summary: The director of 'Rehearsals for a Revolution,' the U.K.'s submission for best international feature at the Academy Awards, on 40 years of Iranian history told through her own life — and how an exile built the film with almost no money.
articles.content:
"Cinema is not just part of my life," begins Pegah Ahangarani. "It's me, actually."

The director and actress grew up on film sets. Both of her parents were filmmakers themselves and immersed their children in the Iranian entertainment industry. Ahangarani became a child star, skyrocketing to fame at just 14 in 1999's The Girl in the Sneakers . "I won a lot of awards," she smiles to The Hollywood Reporter . But even she couldn't have predicted the award-winning success of her debut feature-length documentary, Rehearsals for a Revolution . blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4],[300,251]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Movies Record Number of International and Animated Features Oscar-Eligible This Season Music Don Toliver Postpones O2 Arena Show After Evacuation Due to "Unknown Substance" Released at Manchester Concert

The Cannes-premiering — and L'Œil d'or-winning — project is a poignant reminder of the power of memory. Ahangarani, whose other essay documentaries include shorts I Am Trying to Remember (2021), My Father (2023) and Child Soldier (2024), sketches her entire life story in this latest work. Drawing from personal archives, home videos, street protest footage, newspapers and recorded voices, she retraces more than 40 years of Iran ’s turbulent history. From the late '70s up until the war with the U.S. and Israel, Ahangarani pieces together and narrates intimate recollections from her life — the vanilla scent of her schoolteacher's hair and desperate search for her uncle in videos from the 1999 Iranian student protests among them — that help to form the portrait of a country shaped by political repression, and in constant hope for a revolution.

Personal is the operative word in this co-production between the Czech Republic and Spain. "I want to tell my audience: 'Come and sit with me. I want to share everything with you, even my fragility,'" says its director. As daunting as that task was — Ahangarani has already been arrested and spent time in the notorious Evin Prison, and expects not to be able to return to Iran at the risk of a lengthy jail sentence following the release of this film — she remains steadfast in her belief that using family archives is the greatest weapon at her disposal against the regime. "I realized, 'Okay, these are my materials, these are my tools,'" says Ahangarani. "Because I think these personal archives can stand against the dictatorship, the official version of history that the dictators want us to believe." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Having left Iran in 2022, Ahangarani shares candid reflections with viewers about the guilt she's experienced in the wake of this year's civilian massacres and brutal crackdown on the Woman, Life, Freedom movement back home. From London, where she has been settled since 2023, Ahangarani talks to THR about putting that guilt up on screen — and being selected as the U.K.'s submission for best international feature film at the 2027 Oscars : "When you leave your country, you think you are kind of stateless. You need somewhere to attach. You need a place. You need a land… [Now], there is one place that accepted me."

You grew up in film and TV. You were a child star. But when did you first realize you'd like to direct films yourself?

I grew up in cinema, yes. All of the crew members were like my family members. I called them aunties and uncles. ( Laughs .) I cannot separate myself from cinema. Cinema is not just part of my life — it's me, actually. I started cinema as my main career when I was 14. I acted in one film, The Girl in the Sneakers , and that film became very successful. I won a lot of awards. I was a teenager, and I was super happy. And then a few years after that, I remember I saw some documentaries and I thought, "OK, I'd like to maybe be a documentary filmmaker." I made a few documentaries, but they were very naive. It [was] TV-style documentaries. Then I got familiar with [the] essay style in literature, and then I started exploring that style in some documentaries. I saw some Chris Marker documentaries for example, and Jonas Mekas. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

I thought maybe I should find that style for myself, so six or seven years ago I made a short documentary with this style. I used personal archives and I used my voiceover as a narration, and I started making very personal documentaries. That film became very successful as well. The New Yorker published that documentary. It premiered at IDFA Film Festival and a lot of festivals after that. And then I made another short documentary, same style, and another one again. And then after those three documentaries, I started making this one.

The archive of film and photos you use in this is just incredible. Is it daunting, or were you nervous, crafting an entire project around such intimate artefacts and stories?

Yes, actually. ( Laughs .) I had a lot of concern about it, and not just for this film. […] A few years ago, when I was living in Iran, I went to my grandmother's house, and I found some old family albums there. And I started looking through the photographs, and then I saw one photo. My mom was there. My father was there. I was there too. I was two or three years old, and I noticed a man who was standing next to my father, but his face had been scratched out. And I asked my grandmother, "Who is this person? Why has his face been scratched out?" She said, "He was your father's best friend. He was executed after the revolution because he was a political prisoner." And I realized my grandmother didn't destroy the whole photo. She kept that photo, just scratched that face. After that shocking moment, I realized that maybe my responsibility as a documentary filmmaker is to find these old family photos, this personal footage, and find these scratched-out faces and bring them back to life, bring them back to the frame, and bring them back to our collective memory. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid3' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

After that, I thought a lot about these archives, and I realized, 'Okay, these are my materials, these are my tools.' Because I think these personal archives can stand against the dictatorship, the official version of history that the dictators want us to believe. From that day, I started thinking about how I should use these materials as my facts. […] If you go deeper [into] one photograph, if you focus on it, you can see the part of our history in that photograph. But that wasn't easy at all. When I made that short documentary, I sent it to my mother because my mother was one of the characters, my father was one of the characters, and I had a lot of concern because they might be in trouble after that film. But they were okay. I remember one thing: I sent my film to my grandmother, and I told her, "Okay, I made a short documentary based on the photo that you kept for me." And she said, "Yes, maybe I kept that photo just for you to make this documentary."

This is a co-production between Spain and the Czech Republic, is that right? What work went into getting this over the line? Because using your own photos, films and narration, it strikes me as incredibly inexpensive documentary.

[It was made] with nothing, actually. ( Laughs .) I had a producer [with whom] I made three of my short documentaries, Kaveh Farnam [founder of the Czech Republic's Media Nest], and he's an Iranian independent film [producer] outside of Iran. I remember when I was making a previous documentary, I found him, I texted him, and he joined the project. And that one was like this — I didn't need money because I worked with my personal archives. But I wanted support for distribution [and] things. At that time, I was inside Iran, and I told Mr. Farnum that after this film, if I got arrested or something like that, please publish the film. I needed someone just for publishing. And then when I moved to London, I talked to Mr. Farnum about this feature film, and he said, "Okay, I'm in," and I didn't need any money for that. I just needed a small [amount of] money for my editor [Arash Ashtiani]. The Spain company [Fasten Films]… they found me and they wanted me to make another film for them. And then I told them, "I have one film, it's finished now. I can send it to you, and if you want, you can join this project as well." Right after they watched the film, they texted me and they told me, "Oh, we love the film. We want to join the project." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid4' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

They supported us because we needed some money for the copyright of the music and sound design, and they have a good relationship with a French distributor… Then they sent the film to the Cannes Film Festival, and they have a very good relationship with Cannes because they are French, and everything actually happened after that. But for the process of making this, we didn't need any money.

One standout part of the documentary, for me, is when you're scrolling through some of those harrowing images and videos from this year's protests and you talk about your guilt and trying to compensate for that with the film. What has it been like reckoning with that through these glamorous film festivals?

Everything was very strange because right after the massacre, we were in the process of editing episode five. We wanted to show me [and] my new life as an immigrant, living in exile, and then war happened and massacre happened, and so we didn't know how we should respond [to] these disasters in our film. That was a very complicated situation because I couldn't focus on the film. I told my editor, "Cinema doesn't mean [anything] anymore after all these dead bodies." And then I realized that, "Okay, I should share all these concerns with my audience because this is the only way I should tell them."

But I didn't have any idea that the the film [could] be successful. During the process of making this, it was just me and my editor, Arash, and a little mic, and a very intimate space. I remember the distribution company texted me and told me the director of Cannes, Thierry Frémaux, told us maybe you can be in the official selection. That was very exciting. That day, I just lay down on the sofa in our office… I couldn't handle this much excitement. We realized we can compete with, for example, Steven Soderbergh, because he had a film in Cannes in the official documentary selection. And in Cannes, they told us, "You won the best documentary prize," and I think I'm in the middle of some dream or something like that. Not because my film is successful now, but because I try to show these 40 years of Iranian history and this ongoing struggle of the Iranian people, and everybody around the world now can see this struggle. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid5' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

What do you hope audiences are talking and thinking about after seeing this film?

After the first screening in Cannes, I realized one thing, which was very sweet: When the film finished and people started clapping, many of them came and told me, "We think we love your people as much as you." I thought, 'So this is cinema.' You can show something that people don't have any idea about, and they can resonate with it, and they can feel this struggle. They can feel [for] your people, which is amazing.

Many people, after watching the film, they think they know me very well [and that] they're a friend of mine, which is very sweet. I think the film is successful because I could create a sense of intimacy. Through the narration and through the film, I want to tell my audience: "Come and sit with me. I want to share everything with you, even my fragility."

This film is officially the U.K.'s official Oscar submission for best international feature. What does that mean to you?

That was great news. Not just because of the film, but when you leave your country, you think you are kind of stateless. You need somewhere to attach. You need a place. You need a land. When I left Iran, I thought, "OK, this is just a temporary situation." And then I realized that no, maybe it's permanent. I cannot go back anymore. I should accept my new life, and that was very difficult. When the U.K. announced that they picked our film … I had a feeling like I wasn't stateless anymore. There is one place that accepted me. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid6' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

I'm sure you miss your family so much, but you don't envision a future where you can return?

When I left Iran in 2021, I didn't have any plan to stay outside of Iran. I left my country with just one carry-on to participate in the IDFA Film Festival for my short documentary. And after the second screening, my mother, she was in Iran [and] called me and told me the regime had called her and asked her to interrogate me about the film. She told me, "Stay outside for a while, for one or two months." And then the "Woman, Life, Freedom" movement happened and I published a video to show my solidarity with that movement, and then my mother told me they sent a letter [saying] there is a court order against me. They seized my apartment and my bank accounts in Iran and I realized that I can't go back. If I go back, I have to go to jail. I was in jail for one month in solitary [confinement], but if I go back, maybe I could be in jail for six or seven years or something like that. I decided to stay outside because I wanted to make my film.

articles.content:
In Prime Video’s latest original Christmas romantic comedy, Clashing Through the Snow , Christopher Briney ( The Summer I Turned Pretty) and Michell Randolph ( Landman ) portray rival editors whose relationship takes an enemies to lovers arc during a road trip to New York .

Ryan Mitchell (Briney) and Hannah Hendricks both hear from their boss Jeremy (P.J. Byrne) separately that layoffs loom at Latitude Publishing, where they will compete for a merged version of their roles in the new year. The ambitious employees then both set up secret meetings with prospective authors that could respectively land them the job, but require travel to New York city over the Christmas holiday. The pair exhibit fundamentally different taste in books and what they aim to sell, but their shared love of reading provides them common ground on which to bond when a winter storm forces them together during their grounded travels to the east coast. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article1-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid","mid-articleX","mid-article","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[2,2],[300,250],[620,350],[300,251],[501,282],[3,3],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

“Ryan's sort of an interesting case because he's obviously like, ‘How do we market this and how do we make this sellable and profitable?' But he loves books. There's a big part of his heart — and they get into it in the movie — that appreciates literature, and really he just wants people to read books,” Briney said of his character, who leans more into numbers and trends. “That's what it's about. It's not really about money. It's about exposure. At least that was sort of my approach to it. It’s about, ‘How can we get more people to read books?’ which I admire and appreciate in him.” Watch on Deadline if ( !window.pmc.harmony?.isEventAdScheduledTime() ) { pmcCnx.cmd.push(function() { pmcCnx({ settings: { plugins: { pmcAtlasMG: { iabPlcmt: 2, } } }, playerId: '32fe25c4-79aa-406a-af44-69b41e969e71', playlistId: '0199e506-e642-7728-8264-463efe71337b', }).render("connatix_contextual_player_div"); }); } else { // This should only be get called when page cache is not cleared and it's event time. window.pmc.harmony?.switchToHarmonyPlayer(); }

A good visual representation of Ryan lies in a snapshot of his home, where he has framed photos with Hunger Games author Suzanne Collins and Divergent author Veronica Roth. He also mentions his discovering Fourth Wing author Rebecca Yarros two years after it happened. Michelle’s editor Hannah tends to go for the more niche, Awards-bait books that are high brow.

“She’s a literary traditionalist. I remember when I first booked [the role], I was like, ‘I've got to read Virginia Woolf,’ because she talks about how that's who raised her. I love that Hannah's whole thing is, ‘I just want whatever people are reading to mean something,’ for there to be a real purpose behind it,” Randolph told Deadline. “And I've I've definitely thought about what books would Hannah love and what authors, like Jane Austen. I think that she would read a lot of the classics. Joan Didion. And it definitely made me want to read more classics." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dl-mid-article-inject2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article2","mid-articleX","mid-article","mid","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

In the below interview, the stars also break down their reactions to the script, Briney’s Jim Carrey-like approach to physical comedy, Hannah’s career focus, working with Lukas Gage, Buc-ees knockoff Luc-ees and more:

DEADLINE: Had you both read this script before signing on to the project? What drew you to doing an original Christmas rom com, and especially this one, when rom coms are starting to get rebooted nowadays?

MICHELLE RANDOLPH : I read the script multiple times before I signed on to the project. I actually I have this app called Speechify, and I remember I got the script and I was driving and I was like, 'I just really want to read it right now. 'So I listened to it for the first time with Gwyneth Paltrow reading it/speaking it to me. And then once once I got home, I sat down and I actually went through it, a very different experience, but it's such a joyful, fun script. It's silly. It's absurd. I love [that] both the characters have a real emotional core and very specific personalities. I love this script.

CHRISTOPHER BRINEY: It made me laugh, and I think it's really sweet, but I loved that that comedy was an important character in in this script, and it felt like a fun, challenging project, and it was certainly challenging and certainly fun.

DEADLINE: Chris, I feel like you really leaned into the physical comedy of this one.

BRINEY: I hope it's funny, dude. I might like look like an idiot.

DEADLINE: No, that’s not what I’m saying! Could you talk more about the challenge of that and how it was fun to explore that as an actor?

BRINEY: Yeah, I mean, it was really fun. I think that the first couple weeks on a project, you're always finding your footing, and there was some like physicality to Ryan that that I think somewhere in there I had found, and there were some things that Carlson said about…

BRINEY: Right, there were some Jim Carrey moments, and there was like this scene that we shot at Webster Hall when I'm handing the paper through the [glass barricade], and there was just something about how cool he thinks he is, and how like flimsy he really is that really unlocked a lot of that character for me. It was fun. It was really fun. I loved it.

DEADLINE: Michelle, I wanted to ask you too how you know Hannah's very career focused versus l love life, and I feel like that's just really relatable for a lot of women right now. I'm curious your thoughts and what you wanted to bring out in her to make her more more than just that ?

RANDOLPH: Yeah, I love how ambitious she is and passionate. Books are her life. Her authors — she's so invested in her career. She's a literary purist, and I think that passion in someone is so admirable. I also think that's what makes it really sweet when you can see the moments in the movie when she starts to fall for Ryan because it's the first time she's letting herself not take her work so seriously. It's a protection, throwing yourself into work, it's like, "Oh well, I'm distracted and I don't have time for it, so that's why I'm not with somebody." I think slowly she realizes, "I can have both." There's a balance.

DEADLINE: What was it like filming at Luc-ee’s, which I don’t know if you’ve been to a Buc-ee’s, but how did it compare if you have?

BRINEY: I’ve never been to a Buc-ee’s. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-articleX","mid-article","btf","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() ; });

RANDOLPH: I went for the first time.

BRINEY: Is it good? I mean, I'm familiar with the idea and how awesome it appears to be.

RANDOLPH: It's magical. There are so many Bucky's because I film in Texas most of the year, and there's a bunch. I always pass them on the way to set, and I went for the first time with my cast, and we all got the pajamas, the onesie. We all got Bucky's onesies and all the snacks and it's huge. It’s like Costco where they have gas, they have car washes…

BRINEY: I'm more familiar with like Cumberland Farms and Wawa on roadtrips. I feel like Wawa's maybe junior Buc-ee’s. Wawa's great. I support Wawa.

DEADLINE: What was it like working with Lukas Gage in that smaller role?

RANDOLPH: We've never broken more.

BRINEY: I could not keep it together. I really couldn't. I am sure that there's evidence of that.

RANDOLPH: It's in the movie, which it's like Hannah and Ryan are laughing at the absurdity of what Lukas Gage's character is. But I also know that it was actually Chris and Michelle in that coverage, we broke.

BRINEY: He's so funny, man. He is so good in this movie.

articles.content:
EXCLUSIVE: Following a competitive auction, Lionsgate has landed the rights to the relationship-dramedy Tell Me Everything with Dakota Johnson attached to star and produce. The package had multiple offers with Lionsgate coming in with the winning bid last week.

In the film, when a celebrity couples therapist runs into marital troubles of her own, she encounters a cynical divorce attorney (Johnson) who no longer believes in love. Their unexpected bond causes both to question everything they know about love in this modern tale about marriage, commitment, and relationships.

Johnson, Ro Donnelly and Samantha Racanelli will produce for TeaTime Pictures. Gaelyn Golde penned the script and will executive produce. Chelsea Kujawa and Maria Ascanio will oversee for Lionsgate. articles.title: New GTA 6 Sales Report Claims the Game Is Rapidly Nearing 50 Million Copies Sold
articles.summary: A new report tied to the sales of Grand Theft Auto 6 suggests that Rockstar's latest is already nearing 50 million copies sold. Not long after its launch this past week, Rockstar and its parent company, Take-Two Interactive, revealed that GTA 6 sold 32 million units in pre-orders alone. This led to the game making […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google A new report tied to the sales of Grand Theft Auto 6 suggests that Rockstar's latest is already nearing 50 million copies sold. Not long after its launch this past week, Rockstar and its parent company, Take-Two Interactive, revealed that GTA 6 sold 32 million units in pre-orders alone . This led to the game making almost $4 billion on its first day and, in the process, setting a new record for an entertainment release. And while it seemed feasible that sales for GTA 6 might settle in this range for a bit, it sounds as though they only continue to skyrocket.

According to Rhys Elliott of Alinea Analytics, Grand Theft Auto 6 is estimated to have already sold 44.9 million copies. Of this total, 33.7 million of the game's sales are said to have occurred on PS5, with the other 11.2 million being on Xbox platforms. Assuming that this data is accurate, it means that GTA 6 has already sold an additional 12 million copies in the four days since its arrival on November 19th.

Although Grand Theft Auto 6 has a long way to go to reach the heights seen by Grand Theft Auto 5 (which has lifetime sales of 235 million units), it's astonishing that the game is already rapidly approaching the 50 million milestone. For context, only a handful of video games in history have ever surpassed 50 million copies sold, many of which took years upon years to ever get near this threshold. GTA 6 is clearly going to catapult past this number sooner than any other game in history, and it could do so before the end of this week. At that point, it would be quickly approaching the lifetime sales of The Witcher 3 and The Elder Scrolls 5: Skyrim , both of which are sitting at 65 million units.

What's even more baffling about this success for Grand Theft Auto 6 is that the game has yet to even come to PC. Assuming that GTA 6 had simultaneously launched across consoles and PC, it's safe to believe that the game could have already been well past the 50 million mark. This inevitable PC release , plus the eventual launch of GTA Online in GTA 6 , will undoubtedly only continue to bring in new players, which will drive this sales total even higher. When all is said and done, GTA 6 is on pace to be one of the biggest games in history, which surely sets up Rockstar to continue pouring more resources than ever before into its next project .

How do you feel about these sales so far for Grand Theft Auto 6 ? Did you expect them to be this high, or is the game surpassing all of your expectations? Be sure to let me know for yourself down in the comments section.

articles.title: Inside the 'Pillsbury Bake-Off Classic': A Recipe for Blending Brands With TV (and a Full-Circle Career Moment for Host Drew Barrymore)

articles.content:
The folks behind CBS ' Pillsbury Bake-Off Classic are hoping to make this holiday special an annual Thanksgiving week tradition.

"I feel like this is going to become part of our cultural tradition," says Scott Weintrob, founder of Studio Large Eyes and executive producer of the special. "Every Thanksgiving for the next 10 years, with the Pillsbury Bake-Off as the trigger to Thanksgiving week."

The show is actually a collaboration between CBS and General Mills — which, incidentally, owns the "Bake-Off" trademark in the United States. ("Which is why they cannot call The Great British Bake Off the Bake Off in the U.S. and they have to call it The Great British Baking Show, " says Lisa Balzo, head of brand studio partnerships at General Mills .) blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4],[300,251]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories TV 'Survivor 51' Star Lewis Kelly on His $1 Million Coin Flip and Joining the Cast at the Last Minute TV CBS Inks New Deal to Air Kennedy Center Honors

In developing the special, Weintrob drew on his background in advertising, which has included award-winning work with Rihanna (he designed and directed Amazon’s Emmy-winning Savage x Fenty show) along with Lewis Hamilton x Ferris Bueller's Day Off, reimagining the film’s classic valet scene with Lewis Hamilton, Edward Norton and Ferrari, which went viral. (He also recently directed and produced Mr. T: I Pity the Fool for Netflix and created Orlando Bloom: To the Edge for Peacock.)

Weintrob's company, Studio Large Eyes, aims to create brand-inspired entertainment with the philosophy "entertainment first, marketing second." He says his background crossing both advertising and TV gives him a unique perspective to understand both parties and what their objectives are. "They are quite different," he says. "And they have different approaches. Being able to talk to networks and streamers and also being able to talk to global brands. I had this in-between knowledge because they are different in so many ways but they all are trying to do the same thing, so I was perfectly positioned to be the conduit." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Balzo notes that GM, parent company of Pillsbury, had been interested in the idea of a "big grand spectacle" that would incorporate one of the company's brands. She had already met Weintrob previously at an industry event, and the two began having conversations about some options. "I started talking [with Weintrob] about the history of the Bake-Off, and how it used to be this kind of big grand spectacle that was put on as a live event," she says. "Over the years, we've done various different things with it, and it's become a smaller digital activation. We've also collaborated with the Food Network. I mentioned to Scott that we have been talking about, for years, wanting to bring it back to its full glory. And he pitched this incredible live event."

"What I originally said to them was, I love the format of the Westminster Dog Show as a baking show, a large event as a live, two-hour special focusing on ordinary people doing extraordinary things," Weintrob recalls. They agreed on the idea and decided that Thanksgiving would be a key time for the project to air. "I felt we had the opportunity to go and talk to distributors about making this wonderful event. And that's the key word: It's an event."

Balzo says the concept "felt so perfect" and "felt very serendipitous to me at the time. He had this project in his head that that was so perfectly aligned with Pillsbury and what we were looking to do with the Bake Off." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Back to that trademark: Pillsbury held its first Bake-Off in 1949, when it was called Pillsbury’s Best Grand National Baking Contest. A total of 100 finalists went to New York to compete, and each received at least $100 and kept the G.E. stove they baked on. Eleanor Roosevelt presented the grand prizes, which ranged from $25,000 to $50,000.

In the 1970s and '80s, the show hit TV and then began expanding to other cities, from Honolulu to Houston. Bob Barker hosted the broadcasts on CBS, with prizes set at $40,000 in the 1980s. Winning recipes were published in print advertisements for folks at home. (Fun fact: Peanut Blossoms, those peanut butter-flavored cookies with a Hershey's kiss in the middle, were first introduced by finalist Freda Smith in 1957, and it is one of nine recipes in the Smithsonian National Museum of American History.) In the '90s, Kurt Wait became the first $1 million grand prize, and the first male to win the title. Phylicia Rashad became the Bake-Off ’s first female host in 2000, and then the Bake-Off moved into the digital era along with a stint on Food Network.

Balzo says that baking competitions are immensely watchable because it offers inspiration for viewers at home. "The recipes they're making are so relatable, and I think people are really going to feel that when they're watching" the new show, she said, adding that many brands are trying to get into this space, and for GM, the Bake-Off special offers an "authentic connection" with Pillsbury. "It feels like bringing back something that people have already experienced and want more of, as opposed to trying to advertise through content like this." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid3' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

For 2026's Bake-Off, Weintrob began assembling a production team and then setting up meetings with distributors. "When network TV is involved, the word 'spectacle' is a brilliant word as a reference point," he shares. "It needs to be a spectacle to work on network, and CBS saw just how great the show could be. They were the perfect partner to work with."

With CBS on board, they set about finding a host. Having read General Mills' Wikipedia page "to the end," Weintrob learned that Drew Barrymore had appeared in a Pillsbury commercial (for its pre-made chocolate-chip cookie dough) at age 4. "I called up Pillsbury and said, 'Drew has an incredible daytime show. Drew's gotta be the host,'" Weintrob shares. "[For] the build to a show, it can't just be about the show. You've gotta get people to watch, there is amplification, there is social. This is all the responsibility of myself and my studio. With Drew, the idea was, play the commercial on your [talk] show, and announce it to the world."

Balzo agrees. She cites Barrymore's authenticity and relatability as two qualities that make her a great host. "Drew authentically remembers that experience [of the commercial], and the brand means something to her," Balzo says. "She really cares about that connection and the authenticity to the brand in this partnership, and I think people will see that come through on screen when they watch the special, which is why we're so excited to have her as our host. [In addition], we wanted this to be about more than just baking. We want to tell the stories of a diverse set of people and their backstories and what baking means to them and memories mean to them. And she's the perfect host to pull those stories out of our contestants. It was incredible to watch her on set because it felt like she was having just this intimate conversation with [the bakers]. I think they felt that too." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid4' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Weintrob and showrunner Brielle Cohen watched 250 submissions from home bakers to cull the list down to 24 competitors who all have "incredible" backstories to share. In addition, famed baker and author Amirah Kassem will join Barrymore and celebrity chef judges Christina Tosi and Dook Chase in the special. It was filmed live on Oct. 23, he shares, which meant a tight turnaround for the Nov. 23 airdate.

For her part, Balzo says this was the first time General Mills had done anything "on this scale," so they really leaned on Weintrob and the production team to guide them through the process, though GM did play a hand in everything from creative direction to final casting to set direction to the judges and host. Execs also saw all the cuts and provided feedback. ( Pillsbury Bake-Off Classic is produced by Studio Large Eyes, Pantheon Media Group and Juma Entertainment. Executive producers include Weintrob for Studio Large Eyes, Jennifer O’Connell, Ariel Brozell, Eden Sutley and Martha Chaput for Pantheon, Robert Horowitz for Juma Entertainment and Brielle Cohen is showrunner. Balzo, Kenzie Caron and Eleanor Harkness serve as executive producers for Pillsbury.)

Weintrob says having a strong relationship with brands is going to be important in the future of TV and advertising. "We are not reinventing the wheel," he acknowledges. "Brands and television have always been connected. Pairing a brand with entertainment is the job of someone like myself. I see incredible opportunity because brands have very clear audiences that they want to get towards. This is what I call brand-inspired entertainment, which is there for the new consumer. It satisfies the existing consumer, but it also offers tremendous opportunity to reach a consumer that may not have heard of General Mills, Pillsbury, their cookies, their variety of product. Especially through this family-friendly show, it's perfect for that brand." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid5' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

But, he adds, it's not just matching a brand with a network and assuming the magic will happen. He says there is a lot of listening on his end and working with the brand to understand what they need while at the same time creating something that's right for a distributor and their audience. "You've got to create bespoke entertainment for a brand," he summarizes. "You can't just send them random ideas."

There's also the challenge of the promotional timeline for brands vs. distributors. Brands usually begin working on their promotional campaigns months out, while the distributors work on a shorter timeline, sometimes even just weeks. Weintrob says he worked with both companies to come up with an approach that benefited each of them.

Both Weintrob and Balzo hope this special becomes an annual tradition that families can enjoy for years. And, Weintrob suggests, the special could expand to include Valentine's Day or Super Bowl editions, for example.

"As a brand and especially the Pillsbury brand, the whole family is so important," Balzo adds. "So we wanted to make sure that we created something that could be one of those moments to bring families together around and create memories around."

articles.title: Yahya Abdul-Mateen II Addresses Marvel Future After Wonder Man Cancellation, And It Sounds Promising

The actor is game if the studio is, as he made clear in a recent interview with The Hollywood Reporter. articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Yes, of course Yahya Abdul-Mateen II would play Wonder Man again. The actor is game if the studio is, as he made clear in a recent interview with The Hollywood Reporter . Abdul-Mateen II's take on the character was one of the more unusual updates from the comics to the MCU, as it posited the cosmic superhero was, in fact, still a fictional superhero within the MCU. Simon Williams was merely an actor, but when he got the role of Wonder Man, his secret super powers came to the fore. By the end of the show's first and only season, Simon Williams was now a powered-up Wonder Man, on the run after freeing his friend Trevor Slattery (Ben Kingsley), who had once again impersonated the arch-criminal Mandarin, this time to cover for Simon.

A second season was announced , and then canceled . But like so many Marvel heroes on Disney+ TV shows, Simon Williams is still out there somewhere, and you'd think he'd want to lend a hand when global threats emerge. "If the phone rings, then I’m looking forward to it," he says. "I’m absolutely looking forward to it. We’ll see what happens."

If Wonder Man remains a one-and-done, Abdul-Mateen II, like Nicolas Cage with Spider-Noir , is nonetheless completely satisfied with what he got to do. "No bitterness attached to it at all," he says, when asked if there is any. "I’ve already won. I got to play Simon Williams. I had my turn to do that. People love the show, and because of the [Emmy] nomination, we were still talking about Simon." As far as the potential for more, he's clear what he thinks: "The story is alive, and Simon Williams is. I think we did something really special with that iteration of Wonder Man ." (Not that Simon dying would necessarily be any obstacle to returning in a comic-book universe.)

Yahya Abdul-Mateen II is a man seemingly born to play superheroic and iconic roles. He has the physique, and the range, and has already played two major DC characters with opposite temperaments: Dr. Manhattan in HBO's Watchmen , and Black Manta in two Aquaman movies. The former is all-knowing and aloof; the latter a volatile nutjob. There's nothing to say he couldn't play a different Marvel character, as Gemma Chan has. Indeed, Abdul-Mateen's own filmography suggests a way — he has twice previously played reboots of classic characters made famous by other indelible actors, as Morpheus in The Matrix Resurrections , and Candyman in Nia DaCosta's re-quel. When the Marvel Cinematic Universe inevitably reboots at the end of Secret Wars , he could make it a third-time charm as a new incarnation of another hero.

Simon Williams' story could also continue in a Shang-Chi sequel, given that the master of kung fu is also an ally of Trevor Slattery, and knows he's not the real Mandarin. The actual Ten Rings organization could shelter both of them as needed. Still, there's something quite dramatically ironic about the Wonder Man actor waiting by the phone for his callback, as that's absolutely something Simon Williams would do. Maybe a sequel could go meta, and be about Yahya Abdul-Mateen II the actor becoming Simon Williams the actor becoming Wonder Man the character. Whatever the case, Abdul-Mateen II is fun to watch in anything, so whether Marvel or otherwise, he'll continue to work in great projects for sure. Lucasfilm probably already has ideas, too.

Do you want more from Simon Williams' story? Or could Abdul-Mateen II play another character? Give us your best casting agent impersonation in comments.

articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Crunchyroll is featuring a lot of anime currently airing this season. However, arguably the coolest fight of this year has emerged from one of Fall 2026's hottest anime, and no one expected it, precisely because the series' premise does not initially incorporate action as its main element. The anime, initially dubbed the replacement for Solo Leveling this fall, Overgeared has emerged as a series of its own, delivering some of the best crafting action and now a straight-up action sequence in its latest episode that stands on the same level as major anime such as Jujutsu Kaisen , Bleach , Black Clover , and many others. The surprising element is that it comes from the studio behind One-Punch Man Seasons 2 and 3, which has been dubbed the studio that ruined a masterpiece.

Overgeared has been standing out since the start, initially thanks to its protagonist, who stands out through his desperation. With Grid's main goal being to acquire money and his primary ability revolving around crafting, the series established itself with a different kind of protagonist and action sequences that stood out thanks to their crafting element . However, the series continued to incorporate action as well, given that combat is a core element of MMORPGs. Now, the latest episode features roughly six to seven minutes of action that matches the climactic sequences of a high-budget anime film.

Overgeared Episode 9, titled "Comrades in the Guild," continues the fight between Tzedakah's guild and Malaxus, the leader of the Yatan cult, with Grid joining the raid as well. With Grid possessing the Shield of Yatan, he boosts the confidence of the guild members, and the fight begins, featuring every member playing their role. It starts with the Macho Man delivering close-combat action that is perfectly animated, offering the kind of hand-to-hand combat that the Naruto series has often showcased. Following this, two more characters appear, fighting Malaxus with a sword and a spear. This is where one of the most beautiful shots is captured, as the camera pans across the action, delivering a captivating sequence.

Following this, the characters with projectile abilities attack Malaxus one by one, with every attack visually enhanced. This culminates in the guild's leader, Jishuka, firing a beautiful arrow. However, even that is not enough to take down Malaxus. Fortunately, Grid's mana ability has increased significantly , allowing him to display his main-character energy by unleashing his signature Pagma's Sword Dance and defeating the villain in a perfect closing sequence. Overall, this entire sequence, which lasts around six to seven minutes, is on the level of an animated movie, culminating in a battle where everyone joins forces to take down the main villain, giving their all and risking everything.

This high-quality animation is particularly surprising because this arc isn't even that major, nor is the anime nearing the conclusion of its season. However, the biggest surprise is that it comes from J.C. Staff, a studio that anime fans had given up on due to its reputation for ruining the One-Punch Man anime . It seems that with Overgeared , J.C. Staff is redeeming its reputation, raising hopes that the finale will be even more epically crafted and further establish the series as Crunchyroll's hottest Fall 2026 anime, featuring some of the coolest fights this year has to offer.

John Turturro may have earned some of his biggest paychecks from Michael Bay's "Transformers" franchise, but the actor says there's a danger in doing too many Hollywood blockbusters.

Speaking at the Marrakech International Film Festival about his decision to join the blockbuster franchise, Turturro recalled advice he received from Robert Redford, who directed him in the 1994 film "Quiz Show." "He said, 'It's good to work both sides of the street,'" Turturro said, referring to lucrative studio projects versus more personal, creative pursuits. "You can cross the street, and you can always go back as long as you don't do too much of it in a row." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Turturro explained that spending too much time on commercial projects can come at the expense of an actor's creative instincts. "What happens is you can lose your inner life," he said. "You want to feed your inner life. That's like your fireplace. You want to feed that."

The actor, who played the eccentric Agent Seymour Simmons in four "Transformers" films between 2007 and 2017, said the franchise required a different creative approach than his independent work. "It's not like a fine painting. It's more like when Picasso does the quick sketch type of thing, and you've got to kind of do it like you're playing with your kids," Turturro said. "There's a challenge to that. Can you do that or not?"

He added that "Michael Bay liked working with me because I basically play a version of him in some ways."

The actor also acknowledged — not for the first time — the financial benefits of taking on a major Hollywood franchise. "They pay me a lot more money, so then I can do all these other projects," he said. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Turturro recalled how his children encouraged him to take the "Transformers" role after years of turning down big-budget studio offers. In one instance, he passed on a substantial paycheck for the 1999 superhero comedy "Mystery Men" after his daughter read the script and gave him a less-than-enthusiastic review.

"They offered me a ton of money. I've never made this much money," Turturro said but when he showed his daughter the script she called it "garbage."

At the time, Turturro was also considering a stage production of Samuel Beckett's "Waiting for Godot." After reading the first eight pages of the play together, his daughter had a very different reaction: "This is good. This is very good." Turturro ultimately chose the play, where he earned just $300 a week.

Turtorro concluded with a final analogy: "I consider myself a plumber in my real work, and [commercial movies] are sort of my electrical job."

Turturro's latest project, "The Only Living Pickpocket in New York," also screened at Marrakech following his Golden Star tribute on Sunday night . Directed by Noah Segan and produced by Rian Johnson and Ram Bergman's T-Street, the indie crime drama stars Turturro as an aging pickpocket struggling to make ends meet in a rapidly changing New York City. The film, which also stars Steve Buscemi, Giancarlo Esposito and Tatiana Maslany, premiered at Sundance earlier this year and was acquired by Sony Pictures Classics.

articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google The Half-Life remake just got a major update. When the original Half-Life came out in 1998, it revolutionized the first-person shooter genre. Then in 2004, Valve did it again with Half-Life 2 . Unfortunately, while the Half-Life 3 rumors persist , right now the series remains on ice, much like the rest of Valve's back catalog. In 2020, fans took it upon themselves to release a remake/reimagining of the first game titled Black Mesa . And Valve not only allowed it, but also allowed it to be released on Steam, where it proved to be very popular. To this end, it has nearly 71,000 user reviews on Steam to date, with a 94% approval rating.

Right now, it's on sale for $5, down from $20, but more noteworthy than that, it just got a major update, and this major update added Steam Deck verification. Previously, it was playable on the Steam Deck, but now it is Steam Deck Verified. This means Valve has confirmed the PC game works from start to finish and works well with the built-in display and controls of the Steam Deck. At least this is what it's supposed to mean. Practically, it doesn't always quite mean this because the standard of verification is perhaps not as strict as it should be.

Not only did the game get Steam Deck verified, but it got a major update as well. To this end, there are visual upgrades, engine optimizations, and a complete interface overhaul. The update also notably and substantially improves mod support.

articles.content:
"It's a huge relief," says Hoon Lee of the reaction to East of Eden . "With any production, people work very hard. But I think this one in particular, there was the weight of expectation and wanting to honor the source material that adds a slightly different dimension."

The actor stars as Lee in Zoe Kazan's adaptation of the classic John Steinbeck novel, released last month. The Florence Pugh-fronted series was quickly met with praise. "It almost would've been worse if it came out with a sort of indifference, like met with a wave of shrugging," he tells The Hollywood Reporter . "To be well received the way the project has is obviously the best possible outcome and it's very, very gratifying." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4],[300,251]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Critics' Conversation The Best Fall TV Shows Hurt So Good TV Florence Pugh Was "So Nervous" to Release 'East of Eden' and Still Hasn't Read the Reviews: "It Was Too Much With This One"

The series is very much aligned with the novel, but one of the most significant changes came in the form of the expansion of Lee's character. He'd been given a head's up, but he wasn't sure just how in-depth the story would go until he received the scripts. All he knew was that Kazan and writer Alexander Chee had written a standalone episode for the character, the footage for which ended up being woven into other episodes.

The actor was delighted to see what Kazan had to add and challenges anyone that questions just what the writer knows about the material. "That's a huge risk for Zoe and the production but that actually speaks a lot to the boldness of her interpretation. There's a lot of courage there, not only to put that forth, but to do it for the right reasons," he says.

"I don't think anyone in the world knows this text better than Zoe. Every move she's made, there is a reason for it, and there's a justification in the text," he continues. "She's not somebody that is wildly going off script and going off the range to do what she's doing. It's a 600- to 800-page book. The idea that any of us who have just read it have all of the detail at our fingertips … But Zoe kind of does. She's gone to that level." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

The series, much like the novel, is quite heavy. It's clear from moment one that show isn't holding any punches. It might not be the easiest to watch in one go. "There should be a dosage that's recommended," he says somewhat cheekily. "It is intense."

Below, the actor speaks with THR about expanding upon the character of Lee, Kazan's understanding of the material and how much he loves the character.

What did you think about the decision to add more to Lee as a character?

[Zoe's] interpretation is deeply founded in the text, and it is expanded upon. But that choice, to me, speaks to the central ideas of the book itself, the sort of deep wells of humanism that Steinbeck brings. This idea that if we are going to use this book and talk about the thematics of this book — about what it means to be human and to have agency and to have choice — then it's a totally viable thing to me. To make more human the people that at that time would've been somewhat marginalized or reduced — women, people of color. It's certainly bold, but I think it's in keeping with what she wanted to do for the entire production.

It seems like you've gained a real respect for this material. Was there any anxiety about bringing this to life?

There's always the normal anxiety, which just revolves around variables and questions that you just don't have visibility to at the time. We all could have shown up in New Zealand and hated each other, or we could have realized that we had six dollars to make seven episodes. Those sorts of things. But the added responsibility of the text, that's a challenge I want. I want to have to do a good job because it's important to you and because it's important to other people. Where I knew we would encounter some friction is the more that people love any artwork, anything that's important to them, whether that's novels or movies or people or friendships, the more they protect it and the more they want their self-actualized canonical version to remain. There's certainly a pressure there, but that's just not how I view this situation. I can't convince people to view it my way if they're not inclined to. But I just feel that on its face, the idea of even attempting to create a one-to-one analog from novel to film or novel to television series is just flatly impossible. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

For any story. They're just so wildly different in how they work, and how we participate with those mediums. We create the world in a novel. We not only create every detail of the world based on our own assumptions or preferences, we also create a hierarchy of importance. We create the hierarchy of attention to things. If you resonate with a character, that character looms larger in the story even with nothing changed in the words on the page. A film or a television show are exactly the opposite. It's one collective production's view on what is important and what you have to pay attention to, down to controlling what your eye focuses on. When you think about that level of control, there's no way these things can match up. It's not a task worth pursuing, which is part of the reason why I never watched the '50s movie with James Dean. I knew that Lee was not included in that iteration.

Certainly, that's an omission. I have skin in that game literally. But I also think, well, what an interesting time capsule because in making that choice, Elia Kazan is saying, this is what I think is essential in the story. We have that reading, we have that perspective. In contrast, Zoe is doing the same thing. She's saying, "This is what I think is important in this story and how I feel it, and when I read it, what I took from it." That's what we're supposed to do. There's an illusion that's created, particularly in modern film and TV, that the details of the production, including the people who make it, are larger than the story or larger than the characters. In a book like this, that's not the case. It's much more like theater in that way. But you and I, we could do our own versions of Hamlet. We would be participants in a long lineage of people that have done Hamlet, and the role lives above us. We step into that river and step out. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid3' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

In film and TV, it feels to people like a character and an actor are fused, and that prevents people from reexamining it that easily. We should reexamine it. We should reinterpret, especially important stories and deeply felt stories. We should periodically reinterpret them because that's their value to us, is to re-lens the same issues that we wrestle with in a new context, in our context, in our modern context, and remind us of things that we already feel deeply.

What a wonderful lens to at it. Lee is a character that's an essential to the story, in my reading of it. It seems Zoe agrees and you do as well.

Well, it's nice to have peaked now. There's a lot of clarity. Better now than when I was 28, and it's a long slide down the hill. It's an honor. I love this character. I think the character is just a phenomenally realized human being at a time when I did not anticipate that, which perhaps speaks more to my own lack of awareness and shortsightedness, honestly. It's also a good reminder that we broadly generalize, we coarse grain so many things and that in the detail there's openings to a better understanding of the actual complexity that we're wrestling with all the time and have wrestled with throughout our history. It's easy for me as a person of color to … it's an easy trap to paint with a very broad brush about opportunities I feel like haven't been given, things like that.

I was just talking about this, but when Lee says there's a beauty in the truth, even if it's a dreadful beauty — we are in a time and a place where we have a very difficult relationship with the idea of truth, partially because some people have been betrayed by that and partially because some people think truth is weaponized against them in some way and partially because the truth in and of itself is often difficult to confront. Without creating a foundation based upon the truth, how do we build anything with any integrity? How do we move forward? To bring it down to the most trivial levels, if I look at my own work somewhere and I just pat myself on the back for it, it'll be very difficult for me to get better. There's something very, very beautiful about this idea that in looking at this story and in looking at how Steinbeck was able to humanize his character, it prevents me from having the easy out of saying, "Well, everyone at a certain time period felt a certain way and everyone was… There were just amazing people with incredibly broad understandings of humanity at every point." That's something to remind ourselves that. If you're someone that feels like you're marginalized and struggling, you had allies at every point and maybe they weren't given voice and maybe there weren't many of them, but it doesn't help us to feel like the monolith is out there and could come back at any time. I just don't think that that's fair, and I don't think it's accurate.

articles.title: 5 DC Villain Kids Who Somehow Turned Out Even Worse Than Their Parents
articles.summary: Image Courtesy of DC Comics DC Comics has been around for almost a hundred years and legacy has become one of the most important aspects of the publisher. The legends of the Golden Age created legacies that have stood the test of time, but it wasn't just the heroes that upheld legacies over the decades. Villains would hand down their […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google DC Comics has been around for almost a hundred years and legacy has become one of the most important aspects of the publisher. The legends of the Golden Age created legacies that have stood the test of time, but it wasn't just the heroes that upheld legacies over the decades. Villains would hand down their mantles as well, with groups like the Injustice Society starting legacies of evil that would stand the test of time. Just like the heroes, many villains have also had children, bringing up them up in the game. In fact, sometimes even heroes' children end up going evil, turning heroic legacies into something poisonous.

DC has always done a fantastic job with both villains and legacy. The publisher has used both to create some of the worst bad guys imaginable, antagonists who outdo their parent when it comes to evil. These five DC villain kids are much worse than their parents, showing that some some rot begins in the womb.

Bane and Batman have built a fierce rivalry over the years. It all started back in the '90s, with "Knightfall", when the villain decided to come to Gotham City and destroy the legend that was Batman. He broke the Bat and this began a battle between the two that would see Bane become a Joker-level villain for the Dark Knight. However, as the years have gone on, Bane has shown that there was more to him than just evil. He's a much more complex person than all of that and honestly isn't really all that evil when you compare him to other major Bat-villains.

Bane is the greatest export of Santa Prisca and the country decided that they wanted to use their most famous natural resource. They cloned him and created his daughter Vengeance. While she has never reached the level of popularity of her father, she's an even greater monster than he could ever be. She was created to be a weapon and she loves her work, ripping through everyone in front of her with a glee her father wouldn't.

Prometheus was introduced to readers back in 1997, during the event New Year's Evil . He killed a new hero named Retro and took his place after he had won Justice League membership for one day, all in ploy to destroy the team. He'd end up joining the Injustice Gang, the Legion of Doom, and Deathstroke's Dark Army, using his smarts and skills to become a dangerous foe for any hero that faces him. He's basically the Batman of evil, upholding a legacy of evil that was passed down to him by his parents.

Prometheus's parents were spree criminals, traveling the country, robbing and murdering, creating a secret fortune. After they were killed by the police, their son decided that he wanted to destroy all those who fought for justice, spending the money and years of his life to make himself into the most formidable bad guy out there. His parents were bad, but he is so much worse, surpassing their rather mundane crimes.

Donna Troy is DC's most confusing hero . That's saying something in company where Hawkman exists, with DC's continuity reboots playing havoc with her origin. Troy was already a character who only existed because of retcons – the original Wonder Girl was young Diana, but she was put on the Teen Titans by people who didn't know that (this is one hundred percent what happened), forcing them to create Donna on the fly – and Crisis on Infinite Earths made it even worse, because Wonder Woman was never there to save Donna from the orphanage fire. Instead, she was taken in by the Titans of Myth, the parents of the Greek gods. She was one of their children, in fact, the scion of great power.

In one alternate future, Donna had a child with her husband Terry Long. Robert Long would inherit his mother's power and eventually went mad, becoming Lord Chaos. He then want back in time in order to cement his dominance and make sure that the New Titans of the future couldn't stop him. Donna is a great hero, but her son became a monster, almost destroying all of creation with his schemes.

Earth-Three was the pre- Crisis home of the Crime Syndicate of America, an evil version of the Justice League. This Earth was the opposite of Earth-One; good was evil and evil was good. The Crime Syndicate had destroyed the other "heroes" of their planet, except for one – Lex Luthor. He was married to Lois Lane and ended up helping the Supermen of Earth-One and Two defeat Ultraman in the amazing DC Comics Presents Annual #1 (which I wrote a whole feature about here ). The two of them had a child, Alexander Luthor Jr., and ended up launching him away from Earth-Three during Crisis on Infinite Earths , where he helped defeat the Anti-Monitor and create the singular DC Universe. He took Superboy-Prime and the Superman and Lois Lane of Earth-Two to a paradise dimension to watch reality unfold, a welcome retirement.

Alex and Prime watched as the Earth they saved became dark and hopeless, deciding that the best thing to do was to end it all and start all over again, using the old multiverse as the building blocks for the perfect singular Earth. His plans ended up shaking the entire universe, with countless beings dying in the conflict he started. His father was a hero, but he took after another version of his dad, nearly destroying everything to get his way.

Batman faces the smartest villains around , including one of the oldest threats on the planet – Ra's al Ghul. The Demon's Head was a warrior of the ancient warrior, an unstoppable force of conquest, especially once he discovered the Lazarus Pits. He would found the League of Assassins and try to steer the Earth in a direction that would benefit both the planet and the human race. His plans usually involved mass genocide, but he also promised a paradise after this horrible yet to his mind necessary culling. He involved his children in his plans, grooming his daughter Talia to take his place. She has since fell in love with Batman, had a child with the Dark Knight, led the League, created the spy agencies Spyral and Leviathan, and walked in her father's footsteps.

However, as the years have gone on, Talia has cared more about cementing her power in a world where her father never actually dies and leave her what she believes is rightfully hers. Her plans aren't to lead the world to utopia, like her father, they're just to make sure she has the power she wants. Talia doesn't want a better world, she wants one where she can decide what a better world is.

Which DC legacy villains do you think are worse than their parents? Any on this list you disagree with? Sound off in the comment section below.

articles.title: Why Did Netflix Cancel Mindhunter? David Fincher Breaks Silence on Ending (And What Can Bring It Back)
articles.summary: Throw a rock on the internet and the answer to "What's the best Netflix show ever" will no doubt bring up Mindhunter, the psychological thriller drama series from David Fincher that only lasted two seasons on the streaming platform. Even though in the years since that show went off the air, Netflix has produced plenty […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Throw a rock on the internet and the answer to " What's the best Netflix show ever " will no doubt bring up Mindhunter , the psychological thriller drama series from David Fincher that only lasted two seasons on the streaming platform . Even though in the years since that show went off the air, Netflix has produced plenty of Emmy-winning shows that have been watched for billions of minutes, Mindhunter remains a fixture of their legacy as a TV studio . Billed as being a show with a five-season plan, and the seeds already being set up across the earliest episodes to reveal the show's full arc, Mindhunter was cut short and fans have been asking for more ever since.

David Fincher stopped by the Happy Sad Confused podcast recently, where he opened up about the ending of Mindhunter at Netflix , confirming the myriad reasons why the show didn't continue at the streamer and what fans can do to get the show back (he's only being 98% facetious). In short, the answer is cost and time. "I love the fact that people finally love the show. I'm not scolding. I'm just saying things have a time and a place," Fincher said. "And the best-laid plans led to not an optimal delivery system or schedule. And getting off on that wrong foot put us on the wrong foot for the second season… And I just said, 'I don't understand what those concessions (with Netflix) would be that would grow an audience from 2 million to what? Ten? Twelve? What does it need to be?"

Fincher got into the nitty-gritty of what went into the development and the production for Mindhunter in its first season, confirming that trouble in the early days of filming Season 1 led to the delays that would end up hurting the show completely. The filmmaker noted that working in the traditional structure of a TV writers' room led to troubles with the initial scripts.

"The first season, which I'm very happy with, I was proud of, and we did the best we could and I was learning…I really felt like Mindhunter could do for the things that I had tried to do in Zodiac , could do it in a lab setting, in an interesting petri dish," Fincher said, but lamented that he became the de facto showrunner of the series despite not having that title. "It is so much work. That show was a 90-hour work week when I wasn't directing. And I'm not afraid of a lot of work; to me it's like that's how I know I'm alive when I'm at work. But that first season was a cluster f*ck."

Fincher went on to reveal that while they were filming Season 1 of Mindhunter , a showrunner ("that Netflix really liked, had a great reputation," according to Fincher) and a team of writers were hired to begin developing scripts for Season 2. Since the director was so knee-deep in the series at the time, Fincher didn't have a chance to read them until eight or nine episodes had been written.

"I read these scripts, and I threw them away. It was not our show," Fincher added. "So then it was a mad scramble to, 'Okay, we're starting over; we've got to get eight to ten.' I wanted to have 10 in my pocket before we started shooting. I think we got eight and it was the same kind of clusterf*ck the second time."

Fincher went on to estimate that throwing out the scripts for Season 2 "cost us almost a year," meaning that the gap between seasons for Mindhunter would grow from at least a year to 18 or 19 months. At the end of work on Season 2 of Mindhunter , it appeared like that time between seasons was going to grow to two years before Season 3 might be released. Though major gaps between seasons have become the norm in Hollywood ( Stranger Things took three years between Seasons 3 and 4, and another three between Seasons 4 & 5), at the time Netflix was still making annual seasons for its shows.

"That's when Netflix said, 'Look, we got to be honest with you, there are two million people who love the show, and the show cost $100 million a season. It's basically guys with styrofoam cups in their hands sitting at stainless steel tables getting the rundown. Is there anything you can do so this audience can grow?' And I said, 'What do you mean?'"

Fincher revealed that Netflix asked if changes to Mindhunter could be made, such as making it "closer to CSI " or perhaps find a way to add scenes where "they run after somebody with a gun in their hand." True to his word, Fincher wouldn't make those changes, but as we know, that helped bring the show to an end.

"I said, 'No, I can't. I won't. And I don't think you really want me to.' And they said, 'We don't, but we don't know how else how else are we going to grow this?' So, every time somebody says to me, 'Can’t we bring that back?' I say, 'Here's what I need you to do. You need to go out, you need to make 10 million friends, and you need each of them to send me $10, and then I'll do it."

The FCC plans to vote next month on a proposal to further relax ownership limits on broadcasters, this time targeting a rule that limits the number of stations a company can own in one market.

The proposal would allow for TV and radio broadcasters to exceed those limits on a case-by-case basis and if the agency determines that it will "promote the public interest," with criteria including diversity and localism. Currently, a company can own up to two stations in the same market.
